newsitem.title: USA: FOMC seen sparking big concessions at US 2-yr sale.
newsitem.headline: FOMC seen sparking big concessions at US 2-yr sale.

text.p: With chances high the Federal Reserve will hike rates on Tuesday afternoon, it's an equally sure bet that the Treasury's two-year note auction a bit earlier in the day will garner less-than-enthusiastic demand, players said.

The Treasury is slated to sell $17.25 billion in two-year notes on Tuesday at 1300 EST/1800 GMT. And unless the Fed breaks from its recent pattern, an announcement on any interest rate adjustments will be made at around 1415 EST/1915 GMT.
"It is not a problem, but it creates an event risk," said Kevin Flanagan, money market economist at Dean Witter Reynolds Inc. "It could create nervousness and tepid demand."

Consequently, players said they expect the two-year note to stop-out at above 6.25 percent, possibly as high as 6.30 percent, given that about two-thirds of the market is said to be expecting a rate increase.
When the Treasury announced details of the auction earlier Wednesday, the bid on the when-issued two-year note stood at 6.24 percent. It has since edged up to 6.25 percent.

"The market will back up (more) and we'll see some decent concessions," said Scott Graham, co-head government bond trader at Prudential Securities Inc. "The two-year sector is the least likely place you want to be when the Fed tightens."
Traders were quick to point out that this isn't the first time an auction coincided with the anticipation of a tightening.

"In 1994 (Treasury) did an auction and a half-hour later the Fed raised rates, but we had put in so much premium," recalled Neil DeSarno, head trader at CIBC Wood Gundy Securities Corp. "Is it the same now? I don't think so ... 6.25 percent should offer reasonable value even if the Fed raises interest rates," since most players do not expect a string of rate hikes.
Indeed, earlier Wednesday, sources close to the Fed told Reuters that any Fed action to slow the U.S. economy from its robust pace was likely to involve only small interest rate adjustments.
"Where the market closes Friday night, you will see a backup of five, six, seven or eight basis points," Graham added.

Meanwhile, the Treasury will sell $12.5 billion of five-year notes on Wednesday. That auction should go better than the two-year, since Fed intentions would already have been known a day earlier, traders said.
The when-issued five-year note opened trading at 6.585 percent.
